summary: A proposal defining a data compression mode for the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, which RFC 454 had called HASP mode and promised to define later. The author explains the aim of saving network bandwidth on large file transfers, such as those expected for big machines joining the network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 468 describes a way for FTP to represent repeated bytes and filler with shorter codes. It adapts a compression approach associated with HASP and aims to reduce the amount of data sent.

subtitle: A proposed FTP mode that encodes repeated bytes and filler more compactly.

tldr.problem: The FTP design sought efficient transfer of large files, including printer files, while saving network bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 468 proposes an encoding with byte strings, repeated-byte strings, filler strings and control escape sequences. It adapts ideas from HASP's compression scheme for FTP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines a proposed compressed data mode and explains its intended use; the unit records its status as Unknown.

today: The unit records RFC 468's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It specifies a proposed compressed data mode for FTP.

sections.title: Why FTP Might Compress Data
sections.content:
The RFC says FTP was designed for reliable and efficient transfer of large files. Efficiency means both limiting host CPU work and using network bandwidth effectively. The compressed mode, called “HASP” in RFC 454, had been mentioned there but not explicitly defined.

The author says compression can help printer files, including files sent under remote job entry. Experience with CCN's RJS service showed typical print-file compression by a factor between two and three. The RFC also compares the CPU cost of simple compression with projected network transmission costs.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression can reduce the data sent over the network, especially for printer files with repeated characters. The RFC defines a mode that an earlier FTP document had left unspecified.

sections.title: The Compressed Data Encodings
sections.content:
The RFC describes four forms. A byte string marks literal data bytes; its count must be positive. A replicated-byte string represents a count of copies of one data byte. A filler string represents repeated filler bytes, defined as a space for ASCII or EBCDIC types and as a binary zero for Image or Local Byte Type.

A control escape sequence contains an all-zero byte followed by a control byte. That second byte uses the same coding as the descriptor byte in block mode, including end-of-file and end-of-record indications. The author leaves its further definition open because the block-mode descriptor coding was still in question.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can mark bytes as literal data, copies of one byte, or filler. A separate control sequence carries markers such as end of file and end of record.

sections.title: How HASP Relates to the Proposal
sections.content:
HASP (Houston Automatic Spooling Program) managed batch work and input and output devices in OS/360. Its Multileaving Protocol included compression of transmitted text by encoding repeated blanks and repeated single characters.

The RFC says FTP's compressed mode adapts the HASP compression scheme, but some HASP bit-format details were unsuitable or less effective for FTP. The appendix supplies background on HASP and its multileaving system; the compression scheme is the part relevant to FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: HASP had a method for encoding repeated text characters. RFC 468 adapts that method for FTP rather than copying every detail of the HASP format.
